note: Extends the NIST adversarial machine learning taxonomy across 88 studies and catalogues defence effectiveness by model.
title: A Systematic Literature Review on LLM Defenses Against Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking: Expanding NIST Taxonomy
explain_beginner: Large language models can be manipulated with cleverly worded text that makes them ignore their instructions, called prompt injection, or that talks them into producing content they are supposed to refuse, called jailbreaking. Dozens of research teams have proposed ways to defend against both, but the results are scattered across separate papers using different models and different tests, so it is hard to know which defenses actually work. This review reads through 88 of those studies and organizes them using a taxonomy that the US government's NIST agency built for adversarial machine learning, adding new categories NIST had not covered, such as defenses that rewrite the wording of a prompt at the character or token level before the model sees it, and defenses that ask the model to check its own answer. The review finds a few defenses with strong reported numbers. What it does not settle is whether those numbers hold up outside the lab, since the underlying studies rarely test on live production traffic or report what a defense costs in accuracy elsewhere.
explain_business: For any team running a customer facing chatbot, an internal copilot, or an agent that reads untrusted text such as emails or web pages, this review is a usable shortlist of which defenses have real reported numbers behind them rather than marketing claims, including specific fine tuning and dual model architectures that cut attack success sharply in published tests. That said, the review itself warns that these results come from research benchmarks, not live traffic, and rarely say what accuracy or user experience is given up to get them, so a defense that looks strong in a paper still needs to be piloted against an organization's own inputs before being trusted in production. This matters immediately for anyone deploying an LLM that processes content from outside parties, since prompt injection is already an active attack class, not a theoretical future one, and the choice of defense affects both security exposure and ongoing model performance.
explain_practitioner: The authors systematically reviewed 88 studies on prompt injection and jailbreak defenses for large language models and extended NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy with additional categories, including character, token, and sentence level input perturbation, self reflection checks, decoding steering, defensive pruning, and expanded input and output filtering. Where studies reported numbers, results include Jatmo style fine tuning cutting prompt injection success from as high as 87 percent down to nearly zero while keeping over 98 percent of task performance, and a dual LLM architecture called CaMeL driving attack success to zero against indirect injection on several commercial models. The review's own stated limitation is that these numbers are not comparable across studies, because papers use different datasets, model versions, and settings such as temperature, many do not report the accuracy cost of their defense, and no study in the set tested a defense that combines every strategy the taxonomy now lists.
